cards.explanation: The answer is their words. Job asks, “How long will you torment me and crush me with your words?” Words, friends. Words can get heavy. I think a long speech can weigh more than a full bag of flour.

The answer is True. Job says, “Even if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone.” He is telling his friends that even if he did go astray, that's his to carry. I think he's tired of them acting like it's their business. Nothing like a friend who shows up to a mistake with a clipboard.

The answer is God. Job says, “…it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me.” Bildad, Job's friend, had talked about a net catching the wicked (Job 18:8). Here Job says God drew a net around him. Notice he says it straight to his friends, and he doesn't hold back.

The answer is that God has blocked his way so he cannot pass. Job says, “He has blocked my way so I cannot pass…” A road that just stops is a hard thing to face. And he adds that God has veiled his paths with darkness. That's a blocked way and veiled paths.

The answer is his crown. Job says God has “…removed the crown from my head.” A crown is a sign of honor, and Job says it's gone. Right before that, he says God has stripped him of his honor. It's the same loss, said two ways.

The answer is hope. Job says, “He uproots my hope like a tree.” A tree pulled out by its roots doesn't just lose a branch, it loses what held it in the ground. That's the picture he picks for his hope. I think this is one of the heaviest lines in the whole speech.
The answer is False. Job says God's anger burns against him, and that He “…counts me among His enemies.” Not friends, enemies. I think this is a heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit.

The answer is a ramp. Job says, “His troops advance together; they construct a ramp against me and encamp around my tent.” That's the picture he paints, friends. I bet Job felt like it was a lot of army for one man.
The answer is False. Job says his kinsmen have failed him and his friends have forgotten him. That's not standing by him. Kinsmen and friends both, and I think that stings twice.

The answer is stranger. Job says, “My guests and maidservants count me as a stranger; I am a foreigner in their sight.” These are people under his own roof, and they look at him like he just walked in off the road. I think that would hurt. He's a stranger in his own house.

The answer is that he does not answer. Job says, “I call for my servant, but he does not answer, though I implore him with my own mouth.” Job doesn't just call. He implores. I think that part hurts most.
The answer is little boys. Job says, “Even little boys scorn me; when I appear, they deride me.” That word “even” stands out to me, friends. I think it stings.

The answer is True. Job says, “All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me.” That is two blows in one verse. Best friends and loved ones, both. I think it's one of the loneliest lines in his speech.
The answer is pity. Job says, “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity…” He says it twice. He doesn't ask them to fix anything. I think he just wants them to be gentle.

The answer is True. Job asks, “Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh?” Right before it, he says the hand of God has struck him. Now he asks why they pile on too. I think he can't see why they'd add to it.
The answer is stone. Job wishes his words were written with an iron stylus on lead, “…or chiseled in stone forever.” Whatever he has to say, he wants it to stay. Words in stone don't wash away.

The answer is that his Redeemer lives. Job says, “But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.” After all those heavy verses, that “But” is a turn. Everything around him is falling apart, and he still says “I know.” That's the verse people have held onto for a long time.

The answers are skin and God. Job says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.” His skin is destroyed, and then comes the “yet.” That's the whole hope in four words, friends. He doesn't say he'll see an answer or a reason, he says he'll see God Himself.
The answer is False. Job says, “I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger.” That's “for myself” and “my eyes.” He isn't waiting for someone to bring him the news.

The answer is the sword. Job tells his friends, “…then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment.” He's warning them. I think those are heavy words to say to friends.
